learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of introduction to fastapi in a FastAPI application.
Apply or interpret one example related to what fastapi is.

content.intro: This lesson covers introduction to fastapi within introduction to fastapi. Use the supplied syllabus topics as the coverage checklist, then connect them to the worked example and the verification task.
content.why_it_matters: You will use introduction to fastapi to build APIs whose contracts and behavior are understandable to both clients and maintainers. The practical aim is predictable client-server contracts, resource naming, typed parameters and correct HTTP semantics.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Introduction to FastAPI matters because it is part of introduction to fastapi. In practice, focus on predictable client-server contracts, resource naming, typed parameters and correct HTTP semantics. A framework feature only helps when its assumptions match the application; keep input validation, business policy and side effects distinguishable.

items.title: What FastAPI is
items.text: Begin with the problem what fastapi is addresses. Describe the client, the data it sends, the decision the server makes, and the response that completes the contract. Keep framework responsibilities separate from business rules.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Introduction to FastAPI
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run the example with fastapi dev main.py. Add a test for normal input and an edge case.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For read-only examples, no reset is needed. For any example that writes state, use a disposable local database/test fixture; record the starting state and clean up only lab data. Never use production credentials or real personal data.
content_blocks.limitations: This code is inspectable lesson material, not executed by CodeLeaf. Run it only in a local virtual environment or a separately isolated runner with resource/time/network limits. Security examples are sketches, not complete production authentication or authorization systems.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Adapt the example to cover “What FastAPI is”. Write down the expected success result and one invalid, missing, duplicate, timeout or permission-boundary case that matters for this topic.

task: Create a small reviewable artifact for “Introduction to FastAPI”: explain its goal, cover the listed subtopics, show an example with expected result, then include one edge case and how you would verify it.
hints: Start with “What FastAPI is” and state the required inputs, output and assumptions.
Change one thing at a time; check the official reference and capture the actual response/error instead of guessing.
Include a negative/edge-case check and document which behavior remains untested.
expected_output: A reviewable example or design note for Introduction to FastAPI, covering the PDF subtopics, expected behavior and at least one verification check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a code fragment without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Installed versions, imported types, application structure and external services affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: State assumptions; check the versioned official docs; run a minimal local test and add one failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one happy-path response as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid input, permissions, concurrency, timeouts and cleanup are not exercised by a single request.
common_mistakes.fix: Add focused normal and negative tests and record exact expected status/body.

common_mistakes.why: Even short examples may mutate records, reveal data or affect availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic inputs and a disposable environment; review security, cleanup and rollback before promotion.
